The main process keeps menus, the tray, window creation and native dialogs responsive, and the sync engine's work would block it. `node:sqlite` is synchronous, so a catch-up batch writing several thousand rows ties up the calling thread the whole time. In main, that shows up as the whole app freezing. Full-text search is just as bad: a query across a large corpus has no useful upper bound on how long it takes. Putting the socket and the database in their own process keeps that work away from the UI. Main only sets up the connection once with `MessageChannelMain`, then stays out of the renderer↔engine traffic (`docs/DESIGN.md:306`).

The second reason is crash isolation. If the engine hangs or throws on a malformed frame, main respawns it after a second without taking down the app or the user's windows (`apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts:123`). A related benefit, though it's a reason not to use the renderer rather than main: a `utilityProcess` isn't subject to Chromium's throttling of hidden pages. A spike measured a 5-second timer holding at 5001 ms there while a hidden renderer slowed to about 60 s (`docs/DESIGN.md:2582`). The trade-off is that `safeStorage` only works in main, so the token vault stays there and the engine asks main to read and write the refresh token.
